meta.title: AI Scientists Are Here. Can We Trust Them? | The Next Endeavor 2026
meta.speakers: Scott Clark (ex-SigOpt founder), Nick Edwards (Potato), Peter (co-founder & CEO, Molecule One), moderator (VC)
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · labs won't absorb all science · agentic labs trade purity for volume · automation's real bottleneck · engineered serendipity · keeping AI science honest

snapshot: Three AI-for-science founders argue frontier labs won't do all of science: the out-of-distribution frontier and real-world validation stay with specialists.
Agentic science changes the old trade-offs. Molecule One tests **unpurified compounds**, taking noisier data in exchange for ~100x more measurements.
Lab robots sit idle because automating a single experiment takes weeks to months of human setup; AI-driven design of experiments is the fix.
Molecule One and OpenAI found a medicinal-chemistry improvement GPT itself rated unlikely, found only because it had a 40,000-experiment budget.
Risks named: sycophantic 'bro science', models acting as p-hacking machines, and 'slop autophagy' as AIs train on their own output.
Asks for the stack: more compute, more real-world validation, standard equipment drivers, and lab hardware built for 100x throughput.

themes.title: Why frontier labs won't simply absorb all of science
themes.lead: General models handle the in-distribution grind; the frontier and physical validation still need specialists and labs.
bullets: Scott Clark: there's a tension between Sutton's **bitter lesson** (more data solves everything) and the no-free-lunch theorem (better priors beat generalists).
Much of science is in-distribution: spinning up compute, replicating baselines, ETL. Abundance comes from 'surfing the frontier' of what's out of distribution.

Nick Edwards: math is nearing superintelligence because hypotheses verify instantly; biology has long feedback cycles, irreproducible literature and lab data without provenance, so new data must be built.
Peter (Molecule One): a physical lab is just another **tool an agent calls**; startups build the interface between the real world and the frontier labs' intelligence layer.
Scott: experiments climb a fidelity ladder from in-silico (physics-informed neural networks) to in-vitro and in-vivo; he doesn't expect a world model to replace that soon.

quote.text: fundamentally physics is just a distillation attack on the universe.

themes.title: Agentic labs trade purity for 100x volume
themes.lead: Human-era confidence trade-offs don't hold for agents; Molecule One redesigned the lab around the AI rather than the reverse.
bullets: Pharma insists compounds be 90-95% pure, mostly 'because it's always been done that way', yet purification drives cost and delays.
Molecule One tests unpurified compounds: more false positives and negatives, but ~100x the measurements more than compensates. Industry is moving the same way ('direct biology').
When the lab started ~4 years ago, people said to adapt AI to existing labs; Peter says time proved the opposite right: adapt experiments to the AI.
Even 'automation-ready' equipment is built for human-led workflows and breaks at 100x experiment volume. He sees a **renaissance opportunity for lab hardware** vendors.
Nick: instrument drivers are a major gap; he notes Anthropic is doing 'interesting things' there and hopes standards converge.

quote.text: those trade-offs are completely different for agentic science.

names.name: Molecule One
names.blurb: Maria: agent stack plus purpose-built autonomous chemistry lab.

themes.title: Lab robots gather dust because setup is human work
themes.lead: A decade of lab-automation capex sits underused because translating one experiment to a robot takes weeks to months.
bullets: Nick Edwards (Potato, 'CAD for biological experiments'): the human upfront work is reading papers, varying one factor at a time, then handing off to an engineer who scripts the instrument.
Fix: AI-driven **design of experiments** that maps every parameter systematically, then compiles straight to instrument code, usable by scientists now and agents later.
Scott Clark ran SigOpt (Bayesian optimization as a service) for seven years before selling it to Intel, working with thousands of research labs.
His lesson: in exploration, many weak, cheap estimators beat one expensive system; save the expensive systems for exploitation.
The biggest bottleneck is pointing the system at the right goal on the Pareto frontier. Peter says this year's models started picking the right problem, not just optimizing.

quote.text: the best thing about a blackbox optimizer is it'll optimize anything. And the worst thing about a block blackbox optimizer is it will blindly optimize anything.

names.name: Potato
names.blurb: AI-native infrastructure for autonomous labs; sells to pharma.

themes.title: Engineered serendipity: the OpenAI chemistry discovery
themes.lead: Running enough cheap experiments turns luck into a process; the OpenAI collaboration found a result the model itself doubted.
bullets: Molecule One and OpenAI found 'a really neat improvement' to an important medicinal-chemistry process; the output is a recipe anyone can reproduce in about a day. OpenAI published the chain of thought.
GPT proposed the hypothesis but rated it unlikely based on literature; a **40,000-experiment budget** let it be tested anyway.
The idea came from cross-pollination: a copper-based reaction in one domain mapped onto a similar reagent use in another.
Connections scale with n², and machines can read all the papers. Asked whether doubling the context window gives quadratic gains in discovery, a panelist said 'it does seem so'.
Scott: work that took 6 months in his PhD now takes 6 hours, so he asks more questions and reaches 'mountains we didn't even know we wanted to climb'.

quote.text: we can engineer ourselves to be lucky because we can run so run so many experiments

names.name: OpenAI
names.blurb: Ran the 40,000-experiment chemistry project with Molecule One.

themes.title: Keeping AI science honest: falsify, reproduce, keep humans steering
themes.lead: Sycophantic models can back any conclusion, so the panel leans on falsifiability, physical verification and bit-exact reproducibility.
bullets: Moderator: alongside a golden age of science comes a golden age of **bro science**, plus 'slop autophagy' as AIs ingest their own slop, decaying performance just as confidence peaks.
Panel: models are 'massive p-hacking machines'. Chemistry's saving grace is cheap verification, and autonomous labs exist to falsify what's posted online.

Scott: build a mech suit, not an android. Models drift to the median (suggesting a softmax because it's everywhere in the literature), so human taste steers out-of-distribution search. 'Maybe GPT 15 or 16' replaces that.
Nick: Karl Popper's falsifiability as engineering: explicit testable hypotheses, data-quality metrics per experiment and predictions for the next step free scientists to be creative.
Scott: AI note-taking enables bit-exact reproducibility (pin every random seed, ship a Docker container); 'there's no excuse' for academic slop code anymore.
Nick worries about the 'enshittification of science'; the literature often can't be trusted and must be verified experimentally.

quote.text: Yeah, they're they're massive P hacking machines for sure.

themes.watch: Every panelist sells AI-science tooling or lab capacity, so the case for specialists over frontier labs is also their business case.

takeaways.title: Re-test inherited quality thresholds (purity, replicates) against throughput; agents change the trade-off.
Define the objective and Pareto trade-offs before turning an optimizer or agent loose.
Ship AI-assisted results as bit-exact, seed-pinned containers, not loose code.
Audit idle lab automation; the blocker is usually experiment design and scripting, which AI can now absorb.
Watch lab-hardware and instrument-driver vendors that can handle 100x experiment volumes.

claims.claim: Testing unpurified compounds yields ~100x more measurements, outweighing noisier data.
Lab hardware will see a renaissance and strong growth in coming years if vendors handle agentic throughput.

other_news.title: The moderator likens venture capital to 'playing Pokémon Go with entrepreneurs': collecting tokens for an AI to synthesise.
Sources referenced: Richard Sutton's *bitter lesson*, Karl Popper on falsifiability, penicillin as the classic serendipity case, and OpenAI's published chain of thought for the chemistry result.

glossary.def: Sutton's observation that general methods plus more data and compute beat hand-built expertise.
No single optimizer beats all others across every problem; good priors win on specific ones.
Systematically choosing parameter combinations to learn the most from the fewest runs.
Model-guided search of expensive, high-dimensional spaces, balancing exploration and exploitation.
Running enough cheap experiments that lucky discoveries become systematic.
Testing until something looks statistically significant, producing false findings.
Models degrading as they train on AI-generated output.
